The ART cohort report provides data on patients starting antiretroviral therapy (ART) at baseline and their outcomes at 6, 12, and 24 months. For example, a cohort starting ART in July 2019 would have its 6-month outcomes reported in January 2020, 12-month outcomes in July 2020, and 24-month outcomes in July 2021. Similarly, a cohort starting ART in August 2019 would have its 6-month outcomes in February 2020, 12-month outcomes in August 2020, and 24-month outcomes in August 2021. The report tracks various patient outcomes, including those on first-line, second-line, and third-line ART regimens, as well as those who stopped treatment, died, or were lost to follow-up (LTFU). The percentage of the cohort alive and on ART is calculated using the formula [(H + I + J) / C] 100, where H, I, and J represent the number of patients on first-line, second-line, and third-line regimens, respectively, and C represents the net current cohort. Viral load (VL) monitoring is a critical component of ART management. The number of patients on ART for at least 6 months who received a VL test result is recorded, as well as the number of those with suppressed VL (defined as <1000 copies/mL). The percentage of patients with suppressed VL is calculated as [O / N] 100, where O represents the number of patients with suppressed VL and N represents the number of patients who received a VL test result. WHO guidelines recommend updating the definition of LTFU from 90 days to 28 days or more since the last missed appointment, including missed antiretroviral (ARV) refills in either facility or community settings. This change aligns with the 2020 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Strategic Information. For facilities with electronic medical records (EMRs), additional data can be extracted, such as the number of people living with HIV (PLHIV) eligible for differentiated service delivery (DSD) ART models and those enrolled in these models. Eligibility criteria for DSD include being on ART for at least 6 months, having no current illness, demonstrating good adherence, and showing evidence of treatment success (e.g., suppressed VL or adequate CD4 count). The percentage of eligible patients enrolled in DSD ART models is calculated as [R / Q] 100, where R represents the number of enrolled patients and Q represents the number of eligible patients. Special ART cohort analyses may be conducted for pregnant and breastfeeding women, who require more frequent tracking. These analyses align with maternal and child health (MCH) visit schedules and may include disaggregation by pregnancy or breastfeeding status at 0, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Long-term cohort analyses are also recommended, particularly for patients on ART for five or more years. In such cases, cohorts may be combined into annual ART start-up groups (e.g., 2015 ART cohort) to track outcomes over extended periods, such as two, three, or five years. The ART cohort report includes baseline data for each cohort, with subsequent columns for outcomes at 6, 12, and 24 months. At baseline, data on transfers in, transfers out, substitutions, switches, stops, deaths, and LTFU are not applicable. These outcomes are recorded in the 6-month column and beyond. For example, if a patient transfers into a facility in March but started ART in January, they are recorded as a transfer in at 6 months and included in the net current cohort. Patients who switch regimens are recorded based on the most recent change. For instance, if a patient switches from a first-line to a second-line regimen at month 7 and then to a third-line regimen at month 8, only the switch to the third-line regimen is recorded to avoid double counting. For patients enrolled in DSD ART models, retention is calculated as [X / R] 100, where X represents the number of patients retained on treatment at 12 and 24 months, and R represents the number of patients enrolled in DSD ART models. In summary, the ART cohort report provides a comprehensive framework for tracking patient outcomes, monitoring viral suppression, and evaluating retention on treatment. It supports program management and impact assessment, particularly in facilities with electronic health information systems.
